svg.title: Choosing an Ingestion Tool: Copy Activity vs Dataflow Gen2 vs Notebook
svg.desc: A decision tree that routes an ingestion scenario to Pipeline Copy Activity for raw movement, Dataflow Gen2 for low-code shaping, or Notebook for complex procedural code, with a sub-decision among Copy job, Copy activity, and Mirroring.
svg.text: Fabric Ingestion Decision Matrix — Copy vs Dataflow vs Notebook
Architectural Guide: Matching Ingestion Pattern, Data Volume & Transformation Needs to the Optimal Engine

g.aria-label: What does the ingestion scenario need?
g.title: What does the ingestion scenario need? — The root question: raw movement, low-code shaping, or complex procedural logic.
g.text: STEP 1: What Does the Ingestion Scenario Require?
Classify by data processing requirements, transformation complexity, and team authoring preferences:
1. Low-Code Shaping (ETL) ➔ Dataflow Gen2 · 2. Raw High-Throughput Movement (ELT) ➔ Copy Activity · 3. Procedural Logic ➔ Spark Notebook

g.title: Dataflow Gen2 — Low-code Power Query transformation surface — shape data with joins, cleansing, and custom logic before it lands.
g.text: LANE A: LOW-CODE SHAPING (DATAFLOW GEN2)
Power Query Transformation Surface
• 300+ built-in visual data transformations
• Multi-table joins, fuzzy matching, data type cleansing
• Shape & standardize data BEFORE landing into Delta
Ideal Workload Characteristics:
✓ Business analyst & citizen developer friendly (Power Query)
✓ Small to medium batch datasets (< 50 GB)
✓ Standardizing inconsistent schemas & currency values
✓ Staging lakehouse compute acceleration via SQL endpoint
✓ Direct output binding to Lakehouse, Warehouse & SQL DB
✓ Integrated CI/CD support via Fabric Deployment Pipelines
Recommended for: Classic ETL (Extract, Transform, Load)
Engine & Performance Profile:
• Compute: Mashup container + Fabric SQL staging engine
• Throughput: Moderate (bounded by mashup evaluation)
• Execution: Evaluates query folding against SQL sources
• Orchestration: First-class pipeline activity
• Cost: Standard Data Factory capacity consumption
Summary: Best when non-Spark teams need upfront shaping
Watch-outs & Anti-Patterns:
❌ Avoid for multi-terabyte raw bulk ingestion without shaping
❌ Complex procedural loops are difficult to maintain in M
❌ Staging Lakehouse required for high-performance write
❌ Non-foldable queries fall back to single-container eval
Trap: Forcing complex streaming or ML into Dataflow Gen2

g.title: Pipeline Copy Activity — Fully customizable movement with manual control of parallelism — the default for raw, high-volume movement.
g.text: LANE B: RAW HIGH-VOLUME MOVEMENT (COPY ACTIVITY)
Serverless Parallel Data Movement Workhorse
• 100+ native connectors across multi-cloud & on-premises
• Intelligent Throughput Optimization (ITO): Auto · Standard · Max (4-256)
• Thread-level degree of copy parallelism & ForEach fan-out
Core Architectural Strengths:
✓ Multi-terabyte scalable migrations into OneLake Delta
✓ Serverless elastic compute — 0 cluster spin-up delay
✓ Native binary copy & direct Parquet compression
Recommended for: High-Speed ELT (Extract, Load, Transform later)
Chains seamlessly with Spark notebooks for downstream transforms

g.title: Which data-movement primitive? — Inside Copy Activity's territory: Copy job, Copy activity proper, or Mirroring.
g.text: Sub-Decision: Which Movement Primitive Fits Best?
Choose between standalone Copy Job, full Copy Activity, or Mirroring:

g.title: Copy job — Simplified movement with built-in delivery styles: bulk, incremental, and change-data-capture.
g.text: 1. COPY JOB
Simplified Delivery Modes:
• Bulk Load: One-time
• Incremental: Delta sync
• CDC Replication: Multi-table
Key Advantages:
✓ 0 pipeline configuration
✓ Auto-managed scaling
✓ Multi-cloud & cross-tenant
✓ GA Activator event trigger
Replaces empty poll runs
Best for: Pure data movement
with zero activity chaining
Built-in CDC replication

g.title: Mirroring — Near-real-time database replication directly into OneLake.
g.text: 2. DATABASE MIRRORING
Continuous DB Replica:
• Near-real-time Delta sync
• 0 pipeline or schedule needed
• Replicates source changes
Supported Sources:
• Azure SQL Database
• Azure Cosmos DB
• Snowflake
• Fabric SQL Database
Direct Lake ready in secs
Best for: Operational DB sync
without custom batch ETL
Zero compute management

g.title: Notebook Activity — Procedural Spark code for logic no declarative tool expresses well — APIs, streaming, ML, nested data.
g.text: LANE C: PROCEDURAL SPARK LOGIC (NOTEBOOK)
Full PySpark / Scala / Python Flexibility
• Complex procedural algorithms & custom API pagination loops
• Structured Streaming ingestion & micro-batching
• Deeply nested JSON / XML parsing & ML scoring transforms
Ideal Workload Characteristics:
✓ Rate-limited REST APIs with cursor tokens & exponential backoff
✓ Real-time / streaming ingestion from Kafka or Event Hubs
✓ Complex graph traversal, iterative ML models, or custom libraries
✓ Multi-table transaction orchestration in Delta Lake
✓ Dynamic schema evolution & schema enforcement rules
✓ Parameterized invocation from Data Factory pipelines
Recommended for: Complex Ingestion & Advanced Analytics
Engine & Performance Profile:
• Compute: Fabric Spark Pool (Starter pool / Custom size)
• Startup Time: ~5-10s with Starter Pool instant allocation
• Throughput: Extremely high (scales with Spark worker nodes)
• Orchestration: Run as pipeline activity or schedule directly
• Cost: Spark CU usage (24h smoothed, unless Autoscale on)
Summary: The universal escape hatch for non-declarative logic
Watch-outs & Anti-Patterns:
❌ Do NOT re-code simple flat-file copies that Copy Activity handles natively
❌ Custom Spark code requires testing, dependency & CI/CD maintenance
❌ Runtime errors only surface at execution time (no compile check)
❌ Idle Spark sessions consume minimum node CUs until timeout
Trap: Hand-rolling parallel file copy loops inside Spark

g.aria-label: Trap: tuning throughput without finding the bottleneck
g.title: Trap: tuning throughput without finding the bottleneck — Raising ITO or parallelism cannot exceed the source, destination, or network ceiling.
g.text: CRITICAL TRAP
Tuning Compute Settings (ITO / Spark / Parallelism) Without Profiling the External Ceiling
• Total Achievable Throughput = min(Source IOPS/Bandwidth, Destination Write Speed, Network Throughput).
• Setting ITO to Maximum (256) or scaling Spark nodes against a throttled source database only inflates capacity cost with 0 throughput gain.
Remedy: Always inspect Source Read Time vs Transfer Time in Fabric Monitor Hub before adjusting compute parallelism.
